summaries.gardner: J&J is a 140-year-old incumbent in a mature industry, so it does not fit Gardner's Rule Breaker profile of a top dog in an emerging industry. It does show some of his traits: a strong 30% one-year share-price gain, a well-known brand and a sustainable advantage in patented medicines, but it is not commonly called overvalued and its industry is not emerging.
summaries.buffett: J&J fits many Buffett tenets: an understandable business, 64 consecutive years of dividend increases, high returns on capital (ROIC about 20%), strong free cash flow (about $22 billion trailing) and an AAA balance sheet. The weaker points are talc litigation and a price of about 29 times trailing earnings and 22 times forward, which leaves little margin of safety.
summaries.munger: Munger would value the diversified franchise of patented medicines and devices, the conservative AAA balance sheet and a culture anchored in Our Credo. Inverting, the risks are patent cliffs (Stelara, later Darzalex), drug price regulation and litigation, none likely fatal but all real; at about 22 times forward earnings the price is fair rather than cheap.
summaries.lynch: J&J is a classic Lynch stalwart: a large, steady grower (sales from continuing operations up every year from $78.7 billion in 2021 to $94.2 billion in 2025) that can deliver 30-50% gains over a few years. With a PEG around 3 and almost no insider buying, it fails Lynch's cheapness tests, and it is widely followed rather than overlooked.
summaries.fisher: J&J scores well on Fisher's points for R&D ($14.7 billion in 2025), a strong sales organisation, new products replacing maturing ones (about 25% of 2025 sales from products launched in the last five years) and long-term management. Gross margins have drifted down from 70.3% (2021) to 67.9% (2025), and litigation has raised questions about candour.
summaries.graham: J&J meets Graham's defensive-investor tests for size, financial strength, an unbroken dividend record and earnings growth over ten years (diluted EPS $5.48 in 2015 vs $11.03 in 2025). It fails the price tests: about 29 times trailing earnings and 7 times book value, far above the 15x and 22.5 limits.
summaries.thiel: From Thiel's lens J&J is not a zero-to-one company: it has some near-monopoly drugs (Darzalex in myeloma) and strong distribution, but no single technology ten times better than rivals and no secret others overlook. Its durability comes from a constantly renewed portfolio rather than one dominant monopoly.
summaries.gerstner: Gerstner looks for durable growth, operating discipline and a reasonable price relative to growth. J&J has disciplined operations, accelerating sales growth (guided 7.4% for 2026) and strong free cash flow, but mid-single to high-single digit growth at 22 times forward earnings is not the kind of compounding at a discount he usually seeks, and it is not an AI beneficiary.
summaries.druckenmiller: Druckenmiller focuses on accelerating earnings, rising estimates and catalysts. J&J's sales growth has accelerated and guidance was raised in October 2026, but adjusted EPS guidance ($11.05-11.15) is below January's $11.43-11.63 because of acquisition charges and the stock fell 5.7% on Q3 results, so the setup is mixed.
summaries.smith: J&J matches Terry Smith's 'good company' tests: high returns on capital, a 68% gross margin, strong cash conversion and resilient demand for healthcare, and Fundsmith has held it before. The question for Smith would be price, with a free-cash-flow yield near 3.7%, and the drag from litigation.
summaries.greenblatt: On Greenblatt's Magic Formula J&J has a high return on capital (ROIC about 20%), but its earnings yield is modest: operating income of about $27 billion on an enterprise value of about $627 billion is roughly 4.3% (EV/EBIT about 23). It would rank as a quality company but not a cheap one.
summaries.akre: Akre's three-legged stool asks for an extraordinary business, talented and honest managers, and the ability to reinvest at high returns. J&J has a strong business and solid managers, but much of its free cash flow is paid out as dividends (payout about 62%) or used for large acquisitions rather than reinvested organically at high rates, and litigation weighs on governance.
summaries.pabrai: Pabrai's Dhandho approach seeks simple businesses in temporary distress at low prices with little downside. J&J is simple enough and its permanent-loss risk is low, but after a 30% one-year rise and with the talc settlement largely priced in, it is not a heads-I-win-tails-I-don't-lose-much bargain.
summaries.wood: J&J is not a Cathie Wood-style disruptive innovator: it is a large incumbent. It does touch ARK themes through cell therapy (Carvykti), bispecific antibodies and surgical robotics (Ottava, still in development), but these are a small part of a $94 billion business.
summaries.ackman: Ackman's criteria favour simple, predictable, free-cash-flow-generative businesses with high barriers to entry and strong balance sheets, all of which J&J offers. The gaps are limited upside at about 22 times forward earnings, litigation and drug-pricing exposure, and the absence of an obvious activist catalyst.
summaries.sleep: Nick Sleep's 'scale economics shared' model, where a company passes its cost savings back to customers, does not describe J&J, which uses patents to keep prices high. It is a durable, well-run franchise, but its advantage comes from intellectual property and scale rather than ever-falling prices.
summaries.valentine: Valentine backed young companies attacking huge markets with new technology. J&J serves huge, painful problems (cancer, heart disease, surgery), but it is a mature incumbent rather than a start-up riding a technology wave, so his venture lens fits it poorly.
summaries.nash: Johnson & Johnson is a weak fit for Tom Nash's growth-focused process. It is large, profitable, beats earnings estimates and passes his US-market and size screens, but revenue grows about 6-8% a year, debt ($49.0B) exceeds cash ($20.8B), talc litigation is a major legal threat, and it is not built around a secular trend like AI. On his DCF at a 12% discount rate it is worth well under today's price, and it scores about 60 of 130 on his 13 categories.

b2.evidence: It has raised its dividend for 64 consecutive years and continuing-operations sales grew every year from 2021 to 2025.

integrity.evidence: Management is rational with capital and keeps an AAA balance sheet, but the repeated attempts to resolve talc claims through subsidiary bankruptcies (rejected in 2023 and 2025) drew criticism over candour and governance.

b10.evidence: Market value is about $599 billion after spinning off Kenvue, but large retained cash has gone to acquisitions such as Abiomed whose returns are still being proven, so value creation per retained dollar is solid rather than exceptional.

safety.evidence: At $248.61 the stock trades at about 29 times trailing and 22 times forward earnings and 7 times book value, near the analyst average target, so there is little margin of safety.

fairprice.evidence: About 22 times forward earnings for a high-quality AAA-rated company growing sales about 7% a year is reasonable but not cheap.

mu5.evidence: With 2025 sales spread over oncology, immunology, neuroscience and four device franchises and an AAA balance sheet, few things could make it fail outright; patent cliffs, pricing laws and litigation would hurt rather than destroy it.

ly3.evidence: Trailing P/E is about 29 and forward P/E about 22, well above its single-digit to low-double-digit expected earnings growth (PEG about 3).

ly7.evidence: Insiders own about 0.04% with no notable open-market buying, and the share count rose about 0.5% over the past year.

ly8.evidence: J&J is one of the most widely followed healthcare stocks, covered by more than 20 analysts.

longterm.evidence: It spends about 15% of sales on R&D and bought pipeline companies, while protecting a 64-year record of dividend increases and quarterly earnings guidance.

gr1.evidence: Sales were $94.2 billion in 2025 and market value is about $599 billion.

ni10.evidence: J&J reported positive net earnings in each of the last ten years, including $26.8 billion in 2025, despite large talc and tax charges in some years.

gr4.evidence: It has paid dividends for decades and raised them for 64 consecutive years; the current annual rate is $5.36 a share.
